chief_complaint: sudden pop and feeling of being kicked in back of ankle during basketball game
hpi_details: 35M weekend warrior presenting with inability to push off right foot, palpable gap in Achilles tendon, and positive Thompson squeeze test.
ideas: He thinks another player must have kicked him directly in the back of the ankle during the game, tearing a ligament or giving him a severe sprain.
concerns: He is worried that he will need major surgery and months of bed rest, leaving him unable to work at his active job or ever run again.
expectations: He hopes to be fitted with a supportive walking boot or splint and receive an urgent referral to an orthopedic surgeon.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Achilles tendon rupture evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Achilles tendon rupture is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt immobilization in resting equinus with orthopedic/sports medicine referral for shared decision-making between operative repair and functional rehabilitation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden pop and feeling of being kicked in back of ankle during basketball game
Key HPI features: 35M weekend warrior presenting with inability to push off right foot, palpable gap in Achilles tendon, and positive Thompson squeeze test.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Palpable gap approximately 2-6 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, increased resting dorsiflexion of the affected ankle compared to the other side, positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test with absent plantarflexion, and weak active plantarflexion. Distal pulses and sensation intact.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Achilles tendon rupture.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Achilles tendinopathy (partial tear) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Palpable gap in the tendon.
management_principles: Immediate immobilization in resting equinus (splint or boot) and non-weight-bearing, with ice and elevation for symptom control
Confirm the diagnosis clinically (Thompson test, palpable gap) and with ultrasound or MRI if the exam is equivocal
Refer to orthopedics/sports medicine for shared decision-making between operative repair and functional (early-motion boot) nonoperative management, based on activity level, age, and rerupture risk
Begin a structured, protocol-driven rehabilitation program regardless of treatment choice to optimize functional recovery.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Achilles Tendon Rupture: sudden pop and feeling of being kicked in back of ankle during basketball game. 35M weekend warrior presenting with inability to push off right foot, palpable gap in Achilles tendon, and positive Thompson squeeze test.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Palpable gap approximately 2-6 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, increased resting dorsiflexion of the affected ankle compared to the other side, positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test with absent plantarflexion, and weak active plantarflexion. Distal pulses and sensation intact.
reference_soap.plan: Immobilize the ankle in a splint or boot in resting equinus, non-weight-bearing, with ice and elevation. Obtain ultrasound or MRI if the diagnosis is equivocal. Refer urgently to orthopedics/sports medicine for shared decision-making between operative repair and functional nonoperative management, and begin structured rehabilitation once a treatment path is chosen.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Achilles Tendon Rupture
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for sudden pop and feeling of being kicked in back of ankle during basketball game
Select appropriate imaging (ultrasound or MRI) when the clinical diagnosis of Achilles rupture is equivocal
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: 35M weekend athlete with a sudden pop and feeling of being kicked in the back of the ankle, unable to push off, positive Thompson test.

must_ask.say: Can you describe exactly what you felt—for example, a pop or the feeling of being kicked?

must_ask.objective: Assess ability to push off/walk on toes
must_ask.say: Can you stand on your toes or push off with that foot?
Does it feel like there's a gap or dent in the back of your ankle?

must_ask.objective: Ask about prior Achilles symptoms or steroid/fluoroquinolone use
must_ask.say: Have you had prior Achilles pain, or taken steroid injections or certain antibiotics like fluoroquinolones?

must_ask.objective: Explain surgical versus conservative treatment options
must_ask.say: We'll discuss whether surgical repair or a cast/boot approach is best for your activity level.

history.answer: I was playing basketball about two hours ago when I felt a loud pop in the back of my right heel, and now I cannot push off or walk on it.
It happened completely out of nowhere two hours ago during a pickup basketball game when I pushed off to sprint down the court.
The pain is right in the back of my right ankle and lower calf, right along the thick cord behind my heel. It doesn't radiate up to my knee or down into my toes.
It literally felt like somebody kicked me hard in the back of the leg, followed by a sudden snapping sensation and a dull, aching soreness. I would rate it around six out of ten right now.
It has been steady since it snapped two hours ago, but the sharpest pain was right at the moment it happened.
Putting any weight on the front of my foot or trying to walk makes it much worse. Resting with my foot propped up takes the edge off.
My ankle feels swollen and bruised behind the heel, and the back of my ankle feels strangely loose or weak.
No, I have had no fever, chills, unintended weight loss, numbness, or tingling anywhere in my leg or foot.
I have never had an injury like this before, and I've never had any pain or problems with my ankles or calves in the past.
My friends helped me off the court, put an ice bag on it, and gave me a ride straight here. I haven't taken any pain medications yet.
I was playing an intense game of basketball after a week of sitting at my desk, but I haven't traveled, eaten anything unusual, or been exposed to any sick contacts.
I can't put full weight on my right leg, so I definitely can't walk normally, drive, or go to work without crutches.
I heard an audible pop, and I turned around right away because I was sure someone had kicked my ankle, but nobody was behind me.
I completely lost the ability to push off on that foot, and there is no way I can stand up on my right tiptoes.
Yes, when I touched the back of my heel earlier, it felt like there was a soft dent or gap in the tendon where it used to be tight.
No, I have never had any heel pain, Achilles tendonitis, or any injections into my foot or ankle.
No, I haven't taken any steroid pills or fluoroquinolone antibiotics like ciprofloxacin recently or ever.
I was convinced someone came up behind me and kicked the back of my heel full force while I was jumping for a rebound.
I'm worried this is going to need major surgery and put me on crutches for six months, which would ruin my job and keep me off the court forever.
I'm hoping to get a sturdy walking boot and crutches today, plus a referral to a specialist to tell me if I need surgery.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or gout.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I don't take any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink one or two beers on weekends socially, nothing heavy.
I work as a software engineer at a desk job and live in an apartment with my spouse.
Nobody in my family has a history of tendon ruptures, connective tissue disorders, or early joint problems.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 74/min, respiratory rate 14/min, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, athletic man sitting comfortably on the examination table with the right shoe and sock removed, appearing mildly uncomfortable when moving the right ankle.
Mild swelling and soft tissue fullness around the posterior right lower calf and ankle, with no visible open wound or gross deformity.
Palpable defect and gap approximately 3 to 4 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion with focal tenderness, and a positive Thompson squeeze test with absent plantarflexion on the right calf.
Increased resting dorsiflexion of the right ankle compared to the left, mild tenderness over the retrocalcaneal area, and no knee or forefoot swelling or deformity.
Weak active right ankle plantarflexion against resistance, inability to perform a single-leg heel raise on the right, and preserved dorsiflexion, inversion, and eversion strength.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation across all lower leg dermatomes and the foot bilaterally.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with brisk capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Antalgic gait with inability to push off on the right forefoot and visible limp while avoiding weight-bearing on the right heel.
